subject: Environment
description: Tiger/elephant reserves, Ramsar sites, marine parks

questions.stem: The 'Project Elephant', launched by the Government of India, was started in:
questions.explanation: Project Elephant was launched in February 1992 — nearly two decades after Project Tiger (1973). Goals: protect elephants, their habitats and corridors, address human-elephant conflict, restore migratory routes. India has about 33 notified Elephant Reserves and an estimated 27,000+ wild elephants (the largest population among Asian elephant countries). The Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) is the National Heritage Animal of India (declared 2010).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of India's three biodiversity 'hotspots' recognised internationally?

options.option_text: Western Ghats
Thar desert
Indo-Burma region
Himalaya

questions.explanation: Four of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots extend into India — Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands portion). The Thar desert is NOT a hotspot — hotspots require both high endemism (many unique species) AND severe habitat threat, which Thar's sparse biota does not meet. Hotspot criteria — 1,500+ endemic vascular plant species AND ≥ 70 % original habitat lost.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The 'Silent Valley National Park' is located in:

options.option_text: Karnataka
Kerala
Tamil Nadu
Goa

questions.explanation: Silent Valley is in Palakkad district, Kerala — a UNESCO tentative site within the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve. A proposed hydroelectric project here was scrapped after a major environmental movement in the late 1970s, partly due to threats to the lion-tailed macaque. Declared a National Park in 1984. Adjacent Mukurthi (TN) and Bandipur (Karnataka) are separately protected; Silent Valley sits in Kerala alone.

questions.stem: The difference between a National Park and a Wildlife Sanctuary in India is that:

options.option_text: Only national parks have tigers
A national park offers stricter protection — no human activity beyond research is allowed
Sanctuaries are always larger than national parks
Sanctuaries get central government funding; parks get state funding

questions.explanation: Under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 — national parks (Section 35) have the strictest status: no grazing, no forest produce collection, no human habitation allowed (in principle). Sanctuaries (Section 18) allow some regulated human activities (controlled grazing, collection of forest produce in some cases) and still protect wildlife. Tiger reserves are a separate category — usually include both a core (park-level) area and a buffer (sanctuary-level).

questions.stem: The 'Great Indian Bustard', one of the most endangered birds in India, is the state bird of:

options.option_text: Gujarat
Rajasthan
Madhya Pradesh
Maharashtra

questions.explanation: The Great Indian Bustard (Ardeotis nigriceps) is the state bird of Rajasthan — locally 'Godawan'. IUCN-listed as Critically Endangered; estimated fewer than 150 birds remain in the wild. Major populations — Desert National Park (Rajasthan), pockets in Kachchh (Gujarat), Karera (MP). Big threat: collisions with high-voltage power lines in its flight corridors. Supreme Court in 2021 directed underground cabling in bustard habitats.

questions.stem: Which is India's first Marine National Park?

options.option_text: Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park
Gulf of Kachchh Marine National Park
Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park
Rani Jhansi Marine National Park

questions.explanation: Gulf of Kachchh Marine National Park — Gujarat, established 1982 — was the first marine national park in India. Covers mangroves, coral reefs, mudflats and 42 islands. Gulf of Mannar (TN) was established as a biosphere reserve in 1989 (not originally a 'national park'). Mahatma Gandhi and Rani Jhansi marine parks are in the Andamans.

questions.stem: The term 'conservation reserve' in Indian wildlife law refers to:

options.option_text: A reserved forest managed only by the Forest Service
Buffer land adjoining a national park or sanctuary
A purely private land category
An area where hunting is allowed under permit

questions.explanation: The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2002 added two new categories: 'Conservation Reserve' (public-owned land adjoining existing parks / sanctuaries, serving as corridors or buffers) and 'Community Reserve' (private/community-owned land offered for conservation). These sit lower than parks / sanctuaries in restriction but give formal recognition. Example — Tiruppadaimarathur Conservation Reserve (Tamil Nadu), notified 2005, was India's first.

questions.stem: Which of the following was notified as India's first Biosphere Reserve, in 1986?

options.option_text: Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve, Uttarakhand (1988)
Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, Tamil Nadu–Kerala (1986)
Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve, Tamil Nadu (1989)
Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve, West Bengal (1989)

questions.explanation: The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve was established in 1986 as India's first biosphere reserve, covering parts of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka. Nanda Devi (1988) is the most common wrong answer because it is internationally prominent, but it was notified two years later. Gulf of Mannar and Sundarbans both followed in 1989.

questions.stem: Keoladeo Ghana National Park (Bharatpur), a Ramsar Wetland and UNESCO World Heritage Site, became a conservation alarm when which iconic migratory bird ceased to winter there, with no confirmed sighting in over two decades?

options.option_text: Demoiselle Crane, a common Eurasian winter visitor to India
Siberian Crane, a critically endangered migratory bird
Common Crane, widely distributed across Eurasia and Africa
Sarus Crane, a large resident breeding species of India

questions.explanation: The Siberian Crane (Leucogeranus leucogeranus) once wintered in large numbers at Keoladeo but disappeared from the site by the early 2000s, signalling a population collapse. The Sarus Crane is a year-round Indian resident, not a long-distance migrant, and is a common distractor. Demoiselle and Common Cranes still visit India but were never the flagship wintering species at Keoladeo.

questions.stem: Which of the following Protected Area–State pairings is INCORRECTLY matched?

options.option_text: Namdapha National Park — Arunachal Pradesh, northeast India
Simlipal National Park — Jharkhand, eastern India
Pench Tiger Reserve — Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra border
Dudhwa National Park — Uttar Pradesh, Terai region

questions.explanation: Simlipal National Park lies in Mayurbhanj district of Odisha, not Jharkhand. Because the two states are adjacent, this is a high-frequency examiner trap. Namdapha (Arunachal Pradesh), Pench (MP–Maharashtra), and Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh) are all correctly matched and serve as plausible distractors.

questions.stem: In the three-zone model of a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, which zone is specifically designed for 'sustainable resource use by local communities and experimental research on human–nature interactions'?

options.option_text: Core Zone — strictly protected, no human interference allowed
Buffer Zone — only research and training activities permitted here
Transition Zone — cooperative area for sustainable human use
Eco-Sensitive Zone — a legal buffer under the Environment Protection Act

questions.explanation: The Transition (Cooperation) Zone is the outermost ring of a Biosphere Reserve where farming, settlement, ecotourism, and sustainable resource extraction coexist with conservation goals. The Buffer Zone (middle ring) allows only low-impact research and education; the Core Zone is fully off-limits. The Eco-Sensitive Zone is an unrelated legal instrument under the Environment Protection Act, 1986, included here as a plausible distractor.

questions.stem: Under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, which of the following activities is permissible inside a Wildlife Sanctuary but is PROHIBITED inside a National Park?

options.option_text: Scientific research and ecological surveys by government bodies
Regulated grazing or movement of livestock by traditional users
Photography and filming for documentary or educational purposes
Construction of visitor interpretation and nature education centres

questions.explanation: Under the WPA 1972, the Chief Wildlife Warden may permit regulated grazing or movement of livestock within a Wildlife Sanctuary if it does not harm wildlife. Inside a National Park, once the notification is issued, no rights over land — including traditional grazing — can be exercised, making it legally more restrictive than a Sanctuary. Scientific research, photography, and visitor infrastructure are permitted in both, subject to approval.

questions.stem: Elephant Reserves in India are legally distinct from Tiger Reserves in an important way. Which statement correctly describes this distinction?

options.option_text: Created under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 as a distinct category
Established through executive order with no specific statutory backing
Providing higher legal protection than Tiger Reserves under Project Tiger
Notified only in states where the elephant population exceeds 500 animals

questions.explanation: Elephant Reserves have no statutory basis — they are created through government resolutions or executive orders under Project Elephant, giving them no independent legal force. Tiger Reserves, by contrast, are legally notified under Section 38V of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, conferring a distinct statutory framework with mandatory critical-wildlife-habitat demarcation. This weaker legal standing for Elephant Reserves is a PYQ-frequent distinction that trips up candidates who assume both project-based designations carry equal legal weight.

questions.stem: When Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple (BRT) Wildlife Sanctuary in Karnataka was upgraded to a Tiger Reserve in 2011, it became the first Tiger Reserve in India where the forest rights of an indigenous community were formally recognised under the Forest Rights Act, 2006. Which community was this?

options.option_text: Irula community, known as snake-catchers of Tamil Nadu plains
Soliga community, indigenous forest-dwellers of the BRT hills
Kurumba community, traditional honey-gatherers of the Nilgiris
Jenu Kuruba community, residents of Nagarhole Tiger Reserve forests

questions.explanation: BRT Tiger Reserve (2011) set a landmark precedent when the Soliga community's traditional forest rights were formally recognised under the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 — the first such recognition within a Tiger Reserve in India. The Irula, Kurumba, and Jenu Kuruba are other well-known tribes of south India but are associated with different landscapes and Protected Areas, making them highly effective distractors.
